  relationship_status: Single

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
As a child, Maria had always been close to her younger brother, Carlos. She was only 10 when he was diagnosed with leukemia, and the next few years were a blur of hospital visits, chemo sessions, and endless uncertainty. But one particular moment still haunts her: the day she walked into his hospital room to find him lying in bed, his tiny body hooked up to beeping machines, his eyes sunken and his skin pale. The antiseptic smell and the faint taste of disinfectant that lingered on her lips as she kissed him goodbye are forever etched in her memory. As Carlos's condition stabilized and he eventually went into remission, Maria thought she had left the trauma behind. But now, at 22, she finds herself constantly on edge, bracing for disaster around every corner. When something takes longer than expected – a delayed train, a slow internet connection – she assumes the worst: an accident has happened, someone is hurt, or worse. The uncertainty of those long hospital waits has taught her that delays are always ominous. Even silence can be menacing. If Maria walks into a quiet room or sits in stillness for too long, she starts to feel a creeping sense of dread, as if something is lurking just out of sight. Her friends have noticed that she often fidgets or checks her phone compulsively when they're hanging out in quiet spaces – it's as if she's waiting for the other shoe to drop. When memories of Carlos's illness resurface, Maria often catches herself pushing them away before she can fully recall them. It's too painful to relive those moments, and besides, what good would it do? She's tried to put the experience into words, but her mind goes blank – all that comes up is a jumble of fragmented images and emotions. The taste of disinfectant still transports her back to that hospital room. Sometimes she'll catch a whiff of it on public transportation or in a doctor's office, and suddenly she's 10 again, feeling helpless as she watches Carlos suffer. These physical reactions – racing heart, sweaty palms – leave her shaken and embarrassed. Maria used to be the life of the party, always laughing and joking with friends. But now she feels isolated, set apart from others by an invisible wall. She can't shake the feeling that bad things are just waiting to happen – that she's powerless to stop them. Her accountancy work has become a refuge of sorts, but even there, small mistakes or minor setbacks send her into a tailspin of self-doubt. As she navigates her daily routine, Maria finds herself withdrawing from social invitations and spending more time alone. It's easier that way – fewer chances to get hurt or let others down. Her friends have noticed the change in her, but they don't understand what's driving it. "What's wrong with you?" they ask. "You used to be so happy." Maria just shrugs, unsure how to explain. Lately, though, the loneliness has become unbearable. She's started wondering if things will ever go back to normal – if she'll ever regain her old self. The memory of Carlos's illness still lingers, a constant reminder that bad things can happen at any moment. It's this fear that finally brought Maria to seek help: she wants to learn how to quiet the threats in her head and rediscover some measure of happiness. As she sits in the therapist's office, fidgeting with her hands, she whispers: "I just want to feel safe again."
